paper.instructions:
(i) This question paper contains 33 questions. All questions are compulsory.
(ii) Question paper is divided into FIVE sections – Section A, B, C, D and E.
(iii) SECTION A – Question number 1 to 16 are Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ) type questions. Each question carries 1 mark.
(iv) SECTION B – Question number 17 to 21 are Very Short Answer type questions. Each question carries 2 mark.
(v) SECTION C – Question number 22 to 28 are Short Answer type questions. Each question carries 3 mark.
(vi) SECTION D – Question number 29 and 30 are Case-Based questions. Each question carries 4 mark.
(vii) SECTION E – Question number 31 to 33 are Long Answer Type questions. Each question carries 5 mark.
(viii) There is no overall choice given in the question paper. However, an internal choice has been provided in few questions in all the Sections except Section-A.
(ix) Kindly note that there is a separate question paper for Visually Impaired candidates.
(x) Use of calculators NOT allowed.

questions.stem: A uniform wire of length $L$ and area of cross-section $A$ has resistance $R$. The wire is uniformly stretched so that its length increases by 25%. Calculate the percentage increase in the resistance of the wire.
questions.solution:
Resistance $R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$ ...(1)
New length $L' = L + \frac{25L}{100} = 1.25L = \frac{5L}{4}$
Volume remains constant: $A'L' = AL$, so $A'\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)L = AL \Rightarrow A' = \frac{4}{5}A$
New resistance $R' = \frac{\rho L'}{A'} = \rho\,\frac{\frac{5L}{4}}{\frac{4A}{5}} = \rho\frac{L}{A}\left(\frac{25}{16}\right) = \frac{25}{16}R$ ...(2)
Percentage increase in the resistance $= \frac{R'-R}{R}\times 100\% = \frac{\frac{25}{16}R - R}{R}\times 100\% = \frac{9}{16}\times 100\% = 56.25\%$

questions.stem: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature 40 cm. Find the (i) position of the image formed and (ii) magnification of the image.
questions.solution:
Given $u = -30\ \mathrm{cm}$, $R = 40$, $f = -20\ \mathrm{cm}$
Using the mirror equation $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}$
$\frac{1}{-20} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{30} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{30} - \frac{1}{20}$
$\frac{1}{v} = \frac{2-3}{60} = \frac{-1}{60} \Rightarrow v = -60\ \mathrm{cm}$
Magnification of the image $m = \frac{-v}{u} = \frac{-(-60)}{-30} = -2$

questions.stem: Consider a neutron (mass $m$) of kinetic energy $E$ and a photon of the same energy. Let $\lambda_n$ and $\lambda_p$ be the de-Broglie wavelength of neutron and the wavelength of photon respectively. Obtain an expression for $\frac{\lambda_n}{\lambda_p}$.
questions.solution:
Wavelength of neutron $\lambda_n = \frac{h}{m_n v} = \frac{h}{P}$ and $E = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{P^{2}}{2m} \Rightarrow P = \sqrt{2m_n E}$
$\Rightarrow \lambda_n = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_n E}}$
Wavelength of photon, $E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda_p} \Rightarrow \lambda_p = \frac{hc}{E}$
$\frac{\lambda_n}{\lambda_p} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_n E}} \times \frac{E}{hc} \Rightarrow \frac{\lambda_n}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\frac{E}{2m_n}}\cdot\frac{1}{c}$

questions.stem: (a) Monochromatic light of frequency $5.0 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ passes from air into a medium of refractive index 1.5. Find the wavelength of the light (i) reflected, and (ii) refracted at the interface of the two media.
questions.solution:
(a) $\nu = 5 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $\mu = 1.5$
(i) Wavelength of light (reflected ray): $\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu} = \frac{3\times 10^{8}}{5\times 10^{14}} = 0.6\times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m} \Rightarrow \lambda = 6\times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$
(ii) Wavelength of the light (refracted ray): $\lambda' = \frac{\lambda}{\mu} = \frac{6\times 10^{-7}}{1.5} = 4\times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$
questions.or_stem: (b) A plano-convex lens of focal length 16 cm is made of a material of refractive index 1.4. Calculate the radius of the curved surface of the lens.
questions.or_solution:
(b) Focal length $f = 16\ \mathrm{cm}$, $\mu = 1.4$, $R_2 = ?$
Using lens maker's formula $\frac{1}{f} = (\mu-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$
$\frac{1}{16} = (1.4-1)\left(\frac{1}{\infty} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{1}{16} = 0.4\times\left(-\frac{1}{R_2}\right)$
$R_2 = -6.4\ \mathrm{cm}$

questions.stem: Differentiate between 'diffusion current' and drift current. Explain their role in the formation of p-n junction.
questions.solution:
Diffusion current flows due to majority carriers and Drift current flows due to minority carriers.
Direction of diffusion current: p to n side and drift current: n to p side.
Inside the depletion region, both diffusion current and drift current are present. At equilibrium in a p–n junction, diffusion current in the depletion region is balanced with a drift current, so that the net current is zero.

questions.stem: An air-filled parallel plate capacitor with plate separation 1 mm has a capacitance of 20 pF. It is charged to $4.0\ \mu\mathrm{C}$. Calculate the amount of work done to pull its plates to a separation of 5 mm. Assume the charge on the plates remains the same.
questions.solution:
Given $d = 1\ \mathrm{mm} = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$, $C = 20\ \mathrm{pF} = 20\times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F}$, $Q = 4\ \mu\mathrm{C} = 4\times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$
Initial energy, $U_i = \frac{1}{2}\frac{Q^{2}}{C} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{(16\times 10^{-12})}{20\times 10^{-12}}$
$U_i = 0.4\ \mathrm{J}$
New capacitance when $d' = 5\ \mathrm{mm} = 5d$: $C' = \frac{\epsilon_0 A}{d'} = \frac{\epsilon_0 A}{5d}$
$C' = \frac{20}{5} = 4\ \mathrm{pF}$
Final energy, $U_f = \frac{1}{2}\frac{Q^{2}}{C'} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{(4\times 10^{-6})^{2}}{4\times 10^{-12}} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{(16\times 10^{-12})}{4\times 10^{-12}} = 2\ \mathrm{J}$
Amount of work done $W = \Delta U = 1.6\ \mathrm{J}$

questions.stem: (a) Define current density. Is it a scalar or a vector? An electric field $\vec{E}$ is maintained in a metallic conductor. If $n$ be the number of electrons (mass $m$, charge $-e$) per unit volume in the conductor and $\tau$ its relaxation time, show that the current density $\vec{j} = \alpha\vec{E}$, where $\alpha = \left(\frac{ne^{2}}{m}\right)\tau$.
questions.solution:
(a) Current density at any point inside a conductor is defined as a vector having magnitude equal to current per unit area surrounding that point. It is a vector quantity.
Relation between drift velocity and current is given by $I = neAv_d$ where $n$ = no. of electrons per unit volume.
$I = neA\left(\frac{e\tau}{m}\right)E$, where $v_d = \left(\frac{e\tau}{m}\right)E$ and $\tau$ = relaxation time
$I = \left(\frac{ne^{2}\tau E}{m}\right)A$
From definition of current density $J = \frac{I}{A} \Rightarrow J = \left(\frac{ne^{2}\tau}{m}\right)E$, since $\frac{ne^{2}\tau}{m} = \alpha$
In vector form $\vec{J} = \alpha\vec{E}$
questions.or_stem: (b) What is a Wheatstone bridge? Obtain the necessary conditions under which the Wheatstone bridge is balanced.
questions.or_solution:
(b) A Wheatstone bridge is an electrical circuit. It is used to find an unknown electrical resistance by balancing two legs of a bridge circuit. One of the two legs contains an unknown resistance.
Let the current in galvanometer be $I_g$ and resistance of galvanometer is $R_g$.
Apply Kirchhoff's voltage law in loop ABDA:
$-I_1R_1 - I_gR_g + I_2R_3 = 0$ ....(1)
Apply KVL in loop BCDB:
$-(I_1 - I_g)R_2 + (I_2 + I_g)R_4 + I_gR_g = 0$ ....(2)
In balanced Wheatstone bridge ($I_g = 0$), from eq. (1) and (2):
$I_1R_1 = I_2R_3$ ....(3)
$I_1R_2 = I_2R_4$ ....(4)
eq. (3) $\div$ (4):
$\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{R_3}{R_4}$
This is the condition of balanced Wheatstone Bridge.

questions.stem:
A circular coil with cross-sectional area $0.2\ \mathrm{cm^{2}}$ carries a current of 4 A. It is kept in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude 0.5 T normal to the plane of the coil. Calculate:
(a) the net force on the coil.
(b) the torque on the coil.
(c) the average force on each electron in the coil due to the magnetic field. The free electron density in the material of the coil is $10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$.
questions.solution:
Given cross-sectional area $A = 0.2\ \mathrm{cm^{2}} = 0.2\times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}$, current $I = 4\ \mathrm{A}$ and magnetic field $B = 0.5\ \mathrm{T}$
(a) The net force on the coil is zero in a uniform magnetic field.
(b) The torque on the coil, $\tau = MB\sin\theta$ $[\vec{M} = NI\vec{A}]$
$\tau = MB\sin\theta = MB\sin 0^\circ$, $\theta = 0^\circ$
$[\tau = 0]$
(c) Average force on each electron
$F_m = qV_dB\sin 90^\circ$
$F_m = qV_dB$
Relation between electric current and drift velocity $I = neAV_d$
$4 = 10^{28}\times 1.6\times 10^{-19}\times 0.2\times 10^{-4}\,V_d$
$V_d = \frac{4}{0.2\times 10^{24}\times 1.6\times 10^{-19}}$
$F_m = \frac{1.6\times 10^{-19}\times 4\times 0.5}{0.2\times 10^{24}\times 1.6\times 10^{-19}} = \frac{10\times 10^{-24}}{1.6} = 6.25\times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{N}$

questions.solution:
(a) Graph showing the variation with the frequency: (i) Resistance: $R$ = constant; (ii) Capacitive reactance: $X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi fC}$, $X_C \propto \frac{1}{f}$; (iii) Inductive reactance: $X_L = 2\pi fL$, $X_L \propto f$ (see figure).
(b) Yes, the voltage drop across the inductor or the capacitor in a series LCR circuit can be greater than the applied voltage of the a.c. source because $V_L$ and $V_C$ have opposite phase. $V_L$ or $V_C$ may be greater than $V$. The situation may be as shown in the figure, where $V_L > V_C$.

questions.stem:
(a) State any two properties of a nucleus.
(b) Why is the density of a nucleus much more than that of an atom ?
(c) Show that the density of the nuclear matter is the same for all nuclei.
questions.solution:
(a) (i) Nuclear charge: The charge on the nucleus is due to protons contained in it.
(ii) Nuclear mass: As we may know that the mass of the nucleus is the sum of the masses of the neutrons and protons contained in it.
(b) Nuclear density is invariant of the mass of an atom and hence is constant. The average nuclear density of any atom is about $2.304\times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$.
Nucleus consists of neutrons and protons. And every element has a unique atomic number which is equal to number of protons, which leads to the fact that the mass of nucleus will be different and since different mass results in different density hence nucleus of all elements does not have same density. So the density of nucleus more than that of the atom.
(c) $R = R_0A^{1/3}$
$R_0$ = constant, whose value is $1.2\times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$.
$A$ = Mass number
Density of nucleus $= \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{Volume}}$
$d = \frac{mA}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}}$ {$m$ = mass of proton = mass of neutron}
$= \frac{A\times 1.66\times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}}{\frac{4}{3}\times\pi R_0^{3}A}$
$d = \frac{1.66\times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^{3}} \Rightarrow d \approx 10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$
It is clear that the density of nucleus is constant.

questions.stem:
State the three postulates of Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom.
A hydrogen atom de-excites from level $n$ to level $(n-1)$. Show that, according to Bohr's theory, the frequency of radiation emitted $\nu \cong \frac{\alpha}{n^{3}}$ for large values of $n$, where $\alpha$ is a constant. This result exactly agrees with that obtained from classical physics – one of the successes of Bohr's theory.
questions.solution:
Bohr's Postulates:
(i) An electron in an atom can revolve in certain stable orbits without the emission of radiant energy. The necessary centripetal force for circular motion is provided by electrostatic force of attraction between the nucleus and electron.
$\frac{mv^{2}}{r} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{(Ze)e}{r^{2}}$
(ii) The electron revolves around the nucleus only in those orbits for which the angular momentum is equal to an integral multiple of $h/2\pi$ (where $h$ = Planck's constant) or angular momentum of revolving $e^{-}$ is quantized.
$mvr = n\frac{h}{2\pi}$
(iii) When the $e^{-}$ jumps from higher energy orbit ($E_2$) to lower energy orbit ($E_1$) it radiates energy as a single photon of frequency ($\nu$).
$E_2 - E_1 = h\nu$
From Bohr's theory, the frequency $f$ of the radiation emitted when an electron de-excites from level $n_2$ to level $n_1$ is given as
$\nu = \frac{2\pi^{2}mk^{2}Z^{2}e^{4}}{h^{3}}\left[\frac{1}{n_1^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_2^{2}}\right]$
Given $n_1 = n-1$, $n_2 = n$
$\nu = \frac{2\pi^{2}mk^{2}Z^{2}e^{4}}{h^{3}}\,\frac{(2n-1)}{(n-1)^{2}n^{2}}$
For large $n$, $2n-1 = 2n$, $n-1 = n$ and $Z = 1$
Thus, $\nu = \frac{4\pi^{2}mk^{2}e^{4}}{n^{3}h^{3}}$
which is same as orbital frequency of electron in $n^{\mathrm{th}}$ orbit.
$\nu = \frac{v}{2\pi r} = \frac{4\pi^{2}mk^{2}e^{4}}{n^{3}h^{3}}$
$\nu \cong \frac{\alpha}{n^{3}}$ where $\alpha = \frac{4\pi^{2}mk^{2}e^{4}}{h^{3}}$

questions.stem:
(a) "The wavelength of the electromagnetic wave is often correlated with the characteristic size of the system that radiates." Give two examples to justify this statement.
(b) (i) Long distance radio broadcasts use short-wave bands. Why ?
(ii) Optical and radio telescopes are built on the ground, but X-ray astronomy is possible only from satellites orbiting the Earth. Why?
questions.solution:
(a) The wavelength of the electromagnetic wave is often correlated with the characteristic size of the system that radiates.
Thus, gamma radiation, having wavelength of $10^{-14}\ \mathrm{m}$ to $10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$, typically originate from an atomic nucleus. X-rays are emitted from heavy atoms.
(b) (i) Long distance radio broadcasts use short-wave bands because they can be reflected by the ionosphere of the earth's atmosphere and thus can be send to longer distances.
(ii) With reference to X-rays astronomy, X-rays are absorbed by the atmosphere. But visible and radio waves can penetrate it. Thus, optical and radio telescopes are built on the ground, while X-rays astronomy is possible only with help of the satellites orbiting the earth.

questions.stem:
A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, with one or both surfaces being spherical. The focal length of a lens is determined by the radii of curvature of its two surfaces and the refractive index of its medium with respect to that of the surrounding medium. The power of a lens is reciprocal of its focal length. If a number of lenses are kept in contact, the power of the combination is the algebraic sum of the powers of the individual lenses.

(i) A double-convex lens, with each face having same radius of curvature $R$, is made of glass of refractive index $n$. Its power is : [1]
(A) $\frac{2(n-1)}{R}$   (B) $\frac{(2n-1)}{R}$   (C) $\frac{(n-1)}{2R}$   (D) $\frac{(2n-1)}{2R}$
(ii) A double-convex lens of power $P$, with each face having same radius of curvature, is cut into two equal parts perpendicular to its principal axis. The power of one part of the lens will be : [1]
(A) $2P$   (B) $P$   (C) $4P$   (D) $\frac{P}{4}$
(iii) The above two parts are kept in contact with each other as shown in the figure (first figure). The power of the combination will be: [1]
(A) $\frac{P}{2}$   (B) $P$   (C) $2P$   (D) $\frac{P}{4}$
(iv) (a) A double-convex lens of power $P$ with each face having same radius of curvature, is cut along its principal axis. The two parts are arranged as shown in the figure (second figure). The power of the combination will be: [1]
(A) Zero   (B) $P$
(C) $2P$   (D) $\frac{P}{2}$
OR
(b) Two convex lenses of focal lengths $60\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $20\ \mathrm{cm}$ are held coaxially in contact with each other. The power of the combination is: [1]
(A) $6.6\ \mathrm{D}$   (B) $15\ \mathrm{D}$
(C) $\frac{1}{15}\ \mathrm{D}$   (D) $\frac{1}{80}\ \mathrm{D}$

Junction Diode as a Rectifier :
The process of conversion of an ac voltage into a dc voltage is called rectification and the device which performs this conversion is called a rectifier. The characteristics of a p-n junction diode reveal that when a p-n junction diode is forward biased, it offers a low resistance and when it is reverse biased, it offers a high resistance. Hence, a p-n junction diode conducts only when it is forward biased. This property of a p-n junction diode makes it suitable for its use as a rectifier.

Thus, when an ac voltage is applied across a p-n junction, it conducts only during those alternate half cycle for which it is forward biased. A rectifier which rectifies only half cycle of an ac voltage is called a half wave rectifier and one that rectifies both the half cycles is known as a full-wave rectifier.

(i) The root mean square value of an alternating voltage applied to a full-wave rectifier is $\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$. Then the root mean square value of the rectified output voltage is : [1]
(A) $\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$   (B) $\frac{V_0^{2}}{\sqrt{2}}$   (C) $\frac{2V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$   (D) $\frac{V_0}{2\sqrt{2}}$
(ii) In a full-wave rectifier, the current in each of the diodes flows for: [1]
(A) Complete cycle of the input signal
(B) Half cycle of the input signal
(C) Less than half cycle of the input signal
(D) Only for the positive half cycle of the input signal
(iii) In a full-wave rectifier: [1]
(A) Both diodes are forward biased at the same time.
(B) Both diodes are reverse biased at the same time.
(C) One is forward biased and the other is reverse biased at the same time.
(D) both are forward biased in the first half of the cycle and reverse biased in the second half of the cycle.
(iv) (a) An alternating voltage of frequency of $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is applied to a half-wave rectifier. Then the ripple frequency of the output will be : [1]
(A) $100\ \mathrm{Hz}$   (B) $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$   (C) $25\ \mathrm{Hz}$   (D) $150\ \mathrm{Hz}$
OR
(b) A signal, as shown in the figure, is applied to a p-n junction diode. Identify the output across resistance $R_L$: [1]
Options (A) to (D) are the output waveforms drawn in the figure.
questions.solution:
(i) (A) $\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$
(ii) (B) Half cycle of the input signal
(iii) (C) One is forward biased and the other is reverse biased at the same time.
(iv) (a) (B) $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$
OR
(b) (D) (the waveform shown in the figure: a pulse between $0$ and $+5\mathrm{V}$)

questions.stem:
(i) A resistor and a capacitor are connected in series to an ac source $v = v_m \sin \omega t$. Derive an expression for the impedance of the circuit.
(ii) When does an inductor act as a conductor in a circuit? Give reason for it.
(iii) An electric lamp is designed to operate at $110\ \mathrm{V}$ dc and $11\ \mathrm{A}$ current. If the lamp is operated on $220\ \mathrm{V}$, $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ ac source with a coil in series, then find the inductance of the coil.
questions.solution:
(i) R-C series circuit :
Let applied voltage in a circuit $V = V_m \sin \omega t$ ... (1)
Electric current $I$, on each element is same.
In $\Delta OAP$
$(OP)^{2} = (OA)^{2} + (AP)^{2}$
$V^{2} = V_R^{2} + V_C^{2}$
$V = \sqrt{V_R^{2} + V_C^{2}}$ ..... (2)
If impedance in R-C circuit is $Z$, then $V = IZ$; from equation (2)
$IZ = \sqrt{(IR)^{2} + (IX_L)^{2}}$
$Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + X_L^{2}}$
(ii) When dc source is connected to an inductor then it acts as a conductor because in this case inductive reactance will be zero.
$X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L$
For dc $f = 0$
$X_L = 0$
(iii) Resistance of electric lamp $R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{110}{11} = 10\ \Omega$
If the lamp is operated on $220\ \mathrm{V}$, $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ ac source
$I = \frac{220}{\sqrt{R^{2} + X_L^{2}}} \Rightarrow 11 = \frac{220}{\sqrt{R^{2} + X_L^{2}}}$

questions.or_stem:
(i) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-up transformer and describe its working principle. Explain any three causes for energy losses in a real transformer.
(ii) A step-up transformer converts a low voltage into high voltage. Does it violate the principle of conservation of energy? Explain.
(iii) A step-up transformer has 200 and 3000 turns in its primary and secondary coils respectively. The input voltage given to the primary coil is $90\ \mathrm{V}$. Calculate :
(1) The output voltage across the secondary coil
(2) The current in the primary coil if the current in the secondary coil is $2.0\ \mathrm{A}$.
questions.or_solution:
(i) [Labelled diagram of the transformer: see figure; $N_s < N_p$ as printed]
Principle: Transformer works on principle of mutual induction, in which an EMF is induced in the secondary coil due to the change in magnetic flux linked with it because of change in current in primary coil.
Working : When alternating current source is connected to the ends of primary coil, the current changes continuously in the primary coil, due to which magnetic flux linked with the secondary coil changes continuously. Therefore, the alternating emf of same frequency is developed across the secondary terminals.
(a) Hysteresis loss : Transformer cores are magnetised and demagnetised repeatedly, so lot of electrical energy is wasted in the form of heat in this process. To reduce this loss cores are made of soft iron, which has small hysteresis loop area.
(b) Eddy current loss : The alternating magnetic flux induces eddy currents in the iron core causes heating. The effect is reduced by laminating the core. To reduce electrical energy losses in the form of heat energy, power is transmitted at high voltage upto large distances.
(c) Copper loss : Copper loss occurs in the form of heat energy lost due to the resistance of the copper coils used in the windings of a transformer.
(ii) Yes, energy is not conserve in step up transfer. Energy is lost in a real transformer due to resistance of coil, hysteresis losses eddy current losses.
(iii) Given, $N_P = 200$, $N_S = 3000$, $V_P = 90\ \mathrm{V}$
(1) $\frac{N_P}{N_S} = \frac{V_P}{V_S} \Rightarrow \frac{200}{3000} = \frac{90}{V_S} \Rightarrow V_S = \frac{90 \times 3000}{200} \Rightarrow V_S = 1350\ \mathrm{V}$
(2) $\frac{N_P}{N_S} = \frac{I_S}{I_P} \Rightarrow \frac{200}{3000} = \frac{2}{I_P} \Rightarrow I_P = \frac{2 \times 3000}{200} \Rightarrow I_P = 30\ \mathrm{A}$

questions.stem:
(i) Derive an expression for potential energy of an electric dipole $\vec{p}$ in an external uniform electric field $\vec{E}$. When is the potential energy of the dipole (1) maximum, and (2) minimum?
(ii) An electric dipole consists of point charges $-1.0\ \mathrm{pC}$ and $+1.0\ \mathrm{pC}$ located at $(0, 0)$ and $(3\ \mathrm{mm}, 4\ \mathrm{mm})$ respectively in $x-y$ plane. An electric field $\vec{E} = \left(1000\ \frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{m}}\right)\hat{i}$ is switched on in the region. Find the torque $\vec{\tau}$ acting on the dipole.
questions.solution:
(i) As we know that, when a dipole is placed in a uniform electric field, net force on dipole is zero but it experiences a torque, which can be given as, $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$
This torque rotates the dipole unless it is placed parallel or anti-parallel to the external field. If we apply an external and opposite torque, it neutralizes the effect of this torque given by $\tau_{ext}$ and it rotates the dipole from the angle $\theta_0$ to an angle $\theta_1$ at an infinitesimal angular speed without any angular acceleration.
The amount of work done by the external torque can be given by
$W = \int_{\theta_0}^{\theta_1} \tau_{ext}\, d\theta = \int_{\theta_0}^{\theta_1} pE \sin\theta\, d\theta$
$W = pE\,[-\cos\theta]_{\theta_0}^{\theta_1} = pE(\cos\theta_0 - \cos\theta_1)$
work done by the external torque = change in potential energy
$W = \Delta U = U_f - U_i$
At $\theta_0 = 90^\circ$, $U_i = 0$ and $\theta_1 = \theta$, $U_f = U$
$U = pE[\cos 90^\circ - \cos\theta]$
$U = -pE\cos\theta$
(1) At $\theta = 180^\circ$, $U = pE$ (maximum)
(2) At $\theta = 0^\circ$, $U = -pE$ (minimum)
(ii) Electric dipole moment $\vec{p} = q\vec{\ell}$, $\vec{\ell} = (3\ \mathrm{mm}\ \hat{i} + 4\ \mathrm{mm}\ \hat{j})$
$\vec{p} = 10^{-12} \times 10^{-3}(3\mathrm{m}\ \hat{i} + 4\mathrm{m}\ \hat{j})$
$\vec{p} = 10^{-15}(3\mathrm{m}\ \hat{i} + 4\mathrm{m}\ \hat{j})$
torque, $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E} = 10^{-15}(3\mathrm{m}\ \hat{i} + 4\mathrm{m}\ \hat{j}) \times 1000(\mathrm{V/m})\hat{i}$
$\vec{\tau} = 4 \times 10^{-15} \times 1000\,(\hat{j} \times \hat{i})$
$\vec{\tau} = 4 \times 10^{-12}(-\hat{k})$
questions.or_stem:
(i) An electric dipole (dipole moment $\vec{p} = p\hat{i}$), consisting of charges $-q$ and $q$, separated by distance $2a$, is placed along the $x$-axis, with its centre at the origin. Show that the potential $V$, due to this dipole, at a point $x$, $(x \gg a)$ is equal to $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{\vec{p}\cdot\hat{i}}{x^{2}}$.
(ii) Two isolated metallic spheres $S_1$ and $S_2$ of radii $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $3\ \mathrm{cm}$ respectively are charged such that both have the same charge density $\left(\frac{2}{\pi} \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C/m^{2}}\right)$. They are placed far away from each other and connected by a thin wire. Calculate the new charge on sphere $S_1$.
questions.or_solution:
(i) Electric potential due to electric dipole at point $P$ situated at distance $r$ from mid-point of electric dipole.
Electric potential due to $+q$ charge at point $P$ is $V_1 = \frac{kq}{r_1}$
Electric potential due to $-q$ charge at point $P$ is $V_2 = -\frac{kq}{r_2}$
Total electric potential at point $P$
$V = V_1 + V_2 = kq\left[\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right]$
$V = kq\,\frac{(r_2 - r_1)}{r_1 \cdot r_2}$ ....(i)
From diagram, $PA \approx PN = PO + ON$
$r_2 = r + a\cos\theta$
Similarly, $PB \approx PM = PO - OM$
$r_1 = r - a\cos\theta$
Put the value of $r_1$ and $r_2$ in equation (i)
$V = kq\left[\frac{(r + a\cos\theta) - (r - a\cos\theta)}{(r + a\cos\theta)(r - a\cos\theta)}\right]$
$V = \frac{kq(2a\cos\theta)}{r^{2} - a^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}$   $\{\because r^{2} - a^{2}\cos^{2}\theta \approx r^{2}\ \&\ p = q(2a)\}$
$V = \frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^{2}}$ ...(ii)
Put $r = x$ [from equation (ii)]
$V = \frac{kp\cos 0^\circ}{x^{2}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{p}{x^{2}}$ or $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\vec{p}\cdot\hat{i}}{x^{2}}$
(ii) Given, $R_1 = 1\ \mathrm{cm} = 1 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}$, $R_2 = 3 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}$, $\sigma = \frac{2}{\pi} \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C/m^{2}}$
Charge on sphere $S_1$ is : $q_1 = \sigma \times 4\pi R_1^{2}$
Electric potential, $V_1 = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q_1}{R_1}$
$V_1 = \frac{\sigma R_1}{\epsilon_0}$ & $V_2 = \frac{\sigma R_2}{\epsilon_0}$
Capacitance $C_1 = \frac{q_1}{V_1} = 4\pi\epsilon_0 R_1$ & $C_2 = \frac{q_2}{V_2} = 4\pi\epsilon_0 R_2$
Common potential
$V = \frac{C_1 V_1 + C_2 V_2}{C_1 + C_2}$
$V = \frac{4\pi\epsilon_0 R_1 \times \frac{\sigma R_1}{\epsilon_0} + 4\pi\epsilon_0 R_2 \times \frac{\sigma R_2}{\epsilon_0}}{4\pi\epsilon_0 (R_1 + R_2)}$
$V = \frac{4\pi\sigma(R_1^{2} + R_2^{2})}{4\pi\epsilon_0 (R_1 + R_2)}$
$V = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{R_1^{2} + R_2^{2}}{R_1 + R_2}\right)$
$= \frac{2}{\pi} \times 10^{-9} \times 4\pi \times 9 \times 10^{9} \times \frac{(10^{-4} + 9 \times 10^{-4})}{4 \times 10^{-2}}$
$= \frac{72 \times 10^{-3}}{4 \times 10^{-2}} = 1.8\ \mathrm{V}$
New charge on sphere $S_1$
$V = \frac{kq_1'}{R_1}$
$\Rightarrow q_1' = \frac{VR_1}{k} = \frac{1.8 \times 1 \times 10^{-2}}{9 \times 10^{9}}$
$q_1' = 2 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C} \Rightarrow q_1' = 2\ \mathrm{pC}$

questions.stem:
(i) A ray of light passes through a triangular prism. Show graphically, how the angle of deviation varies with the angle of incidence? Hence define the angle of minimum deviation.
(ii) A ray of light is incident normally on a refracting face of a prism of prism angle $A$ and suffers a deviation of angle $\delta$. Prove that the refractive index $n$ of the material of the prism is given by $n = \frac{\sin(A + \delta)}{\sin A}$.
(iii) The refractive index of the material of a prism is $\sqrt{2}$. If the refracting angle of the prism is $60^\circ$, find the
(1) Angle of minimum deviation, and
(2) Angle of incidence.
questions.solution:
(i) [Graph of $\delta$ versus $i$ with minimum at $i = e$: see figure]
(ii) [Prism diagram: see figure]
Using Snell's law at $Q$
$n \sin A = 1 \sin e$
$\because e = A + \delta$
$n = \frac{\sin e}{\sin A}$
$n = \frac{\sin(A + \delta)}{\sin A}$
(iii) (1) $n = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_{min}}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$
$\sqrt{2} = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{60^\circ + \delta_{min}}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{60^\circ}{2}\right)}$
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \sin\left(\frac{60^\circ + \delta_{min}}{2}\right)$
$\sin 45^\circ = \sin\left(\frac{60^\circ + \delta_{min}}{2}\right)$
$45^\circ = \frac{60^\circ + \delta_{min}}{2}$
$\delta_{min} = 30^\circ$
(2) $\delta = i + e - A$
$\delta_{min} = 2i - A$
$30^\circ = 2i - 60^\circ$
$i = 45^\circ$
questions.or_stem:
(i) State Huygens' principle. A plane wave is incident at an angle $i$ on a reflecting surface. Construct the corresponding reflected wavefront. Using this diagram, prove that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence.
(ii) What are the coherent sources of light ? Can two independent sodium lamps act like coherent sources ? Explain.
(iii) A beam of light consisting of a known wavelength $520\ \mathrm{nm}$ and an unknown wavelength $\lambda$, used in Young's double slit experiment produces two interference patterns such that the fourth bright fringe of unknown wavelength coincides with the fifth bright fringe of known wavelength. Find the value of $\lambda$.
questions.or_solution:
(i) Huygen's Principle:
Huygen's principle gives the geometrical construction of wave front.
(a) Each point on the given wavefront (Primary wavefront) will act as a new source of disturbance called the secondary wavelets.
(b) Only the forward envelop enclosing the tangents at the secondary wavelets gives the new position of the wavefront called secondary wavefront.
[Diagram of reflected wavefront: see figure]
Let speed of the wave in the medium be $v$
Let the time taken by the wave front, to advance from point $B$ to point $C$ is $\tau$
Hence $BC = v\tau$
Let $CE$ represent the reflected wave front, Distance $AE = v\tau = BC$
$\Delta AEC$ and $\Delta ABC$ are congruent
$\therefore \angle ABC = \angle AEC (90^\circ)$
$AC = AC$
$AE = BC$,
So, $\angle BAC = \angle ECA$ (by C.P.C.T.)
$\Rightarrow \angle i = \angle r$ (proved) [2]
(ii) The source which emits a light wave with the same frequency, wavelength and phase or having a constant phase difference is known as a coherent source.
No, Two independent sources of light cannot be coherent because they cannot emit wave continuously.
(iii) $n_1\lambda_1 = n_2\lambda_2$
$4\lambda = 5 \times 520\ \mathrm{nm}$
$\lambda = 5 \times 130\ \mathrm{nm}$
$\lambda = 650\ \mathrm{nm}$
